title: Finite subsets of a comodule lie in finite-dimensional subcomodules
statement: Let $k$ be a field [def-weil-field] and let $C$ be a $k$-vector space with linear maps $\Delta:C\to C\otimes_k C$ and $\epsilon:C\to k$ satisfying coassociativity and both counit identities; tensor products use [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. A right $C$-comodule is a $k$-vector space $M$ with a linear map $\rho:M\to M\otimes_k C$ satisfying $(\rho\otimes1_C)\rho=(1_M\otimes\Delta)\rho$ and $(1_M\otimes\epsilon)\rho=1_M$, under the canonical associativity and unit identifications. For every finite subset $T\subset M$, there is a finite-dimensional [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace] $k$-linear subspace $V\subset M$ containing $T$ and a right $C$-comodule structure $\rho_V:V\to V\otimes_k C$ for which the inclusion $i:V\hookrightarrow M$ satisfies $(i\otimes1_C)\rho_V=\rho i$. The zero comodule and the empty subset are allowed. No algebra structure on $C$ or cocommutativity is assumed.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86; general coalgebra/comodule definitions in §9(d), printed p.174. The proof of Proposition 4.7 uses only the coassociativity and counit identities, so applies to every coalgebra.

proof.text: Choose a $k$-basis $(e_j)_{j\in J}$ of $C$ using [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-basis-through-vector] with the empty independent set. Write $\lambda_j:C\to k$ for its coordinate functional: on a finite basis expansion it returns the coefficient of $e_j$. This is linear and $\lambda_j(e_l)=\delta_{jl}$. By [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], every $\rho(t)$ is a finite sum of pure tensors. Expanding their second factors in this basis and collecting terms gives $\rho(t)=\sum_{j\in S_t}m_{tj}\otimes e_j$ for a finite $S_t\subset J$, for each $t\in T$. Put $m_{tj}=0$ outside $S_t$. Applying the bilinear contraction $x\otimes c\mapsto\lambda_j(c)x$, supplied by the tensor universal property, shows that these coefficients are $m_{tj}=(1_M\otimes\lambda_j)\rho(t)$.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86 (PDF p.98), coefficient-comparison proof; coalgebra and comodule identities in §9(d), printed p.174 (PDF p.186).

proof.text: For $t\in T$ and $l\in J$, coassociativity gives $\sum_{j\in S_t}\rho(m_{tj})\otimes e_j=\sum_{j\in S_t}m_{tj}\otimes\Delta(e_j)$ in $M\otimes C\otimes C$. Apply $1_M\otimes1_C\otimes\lambda_l$, the linear contraction furnished by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. The left side becomes $\rho(m_{tl})$ and the right side becomes $\sum_{j\in S_t}m_{tj}\otimes d_{jl}$, where $d_{jl}=(1_C\otimes\lambda_l)\Delta(e_j)\in C$. Consequently $\rho(m_{tl})=\sum_{j\in S_t}m_{tj}\otimes d_{jl}$. This is Milne's coefficient identity (26), with the second and third tensor factors kept in the right-comodule order.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86 (PDF p.98), coefficient-comparison proof; coalgebra and comodule identities in §9(d), printed p.174 (PDF p.186).

proof.text: Let $V\subset M$ be the span of the finite set $\{m_{tj}:t\in T,\ j\in S_t\}$. It is finite-dimensional by [def-weil-finite-dimensional-subspace]. Counitality gives $t=\sum_{j\in S_t}\epsilon(e_j)m_{tj}$, so $T\subset V$. Write $i:V\hookrightarrow M$ and $J_C=i\otimes1_C$. Step 2 expresses the image under $\rho$ of every generator of $V$ as a sum of tensors whose first factors lie in $V$. Linearity then gives $\rho(i(V))\subset\operatorname{im}(J_C)$: for a finite linear combination of generators, take the same linear combination of their displayed preimages in $V\otimes C$. Here tensor maps and their linearity are those of [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product].

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86 (PDF p.98), coefficient-comparison proof; coalgebra and comodule identities in §9(d), printed p.174 (PDF p.186).

proof.text: Choose a basis of $V$, and extend its image under $i$ to a basis of $M$, using [lem-weil-pbc-vector-space-basis-through-vector] twice. The image is independent because $i$ is injective: a zero linear combination in $M$ is the same zero linear combination in $V$. Define a linear map $p:M\to V$ by sending the extended basis vectors in $i(V)$ back to their basis vectors of $V$ and all remaining basis vectors to zero. Finite basis expansions give $pi=1_V$. Thus, for every vector space $D$, the maps $i\otimes1_D$ and $p\otimes1_D$ compose to the identity on pure tensors and hence on all tensors by [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]; in particular $i\otimes1_D$ is injective. Define $\rho_V=(p\otimes1_C)\rho i$. Step 3 gives $(i\otimes1_C)\rho_V=\rho i$: if $\rho(i(v))=J_C(z)$, then $J_C(p\otimes1_C)J_C(z)=J_C(z)$.

source.place: Proposition 4.7, printed p.86 (PDF p.98), coefficient-comparison proof; coalgebra and comodule identities in §9(d), printed p.174 (PDF p.186).

proof.text: It remains to check the identities for $\rho_V$, not merely stability of its image. After composition with the injective map $i\otimes1_C\otimes1_C$ of step 4, $(\rho_V\otimes1_C)\rho_V$ becomes $(\rho\otimes1_C)\rho i$, and $(1_V\otimes\Delta)\rho_V$ becomes $(1_M\otimes\Delta)\rho i$. These formulas follow on pure tensors from $(i\otimes1_C)\rho_V=\rho i$ and extend by linearity, using [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product]. Coassociativity on $M$ equates the two results, and injectivity cancels the inclusion. Similarly $i(1_V\otimes\epsilon)\rho_V=(1_M\otimes\epsilon)\rho i=i$, so injectivity of $i$ proves counitality. We have the required comodule and inclusion. For $T=\emptyset$ the generating set is empty and $V=0$; for $M=0$ the same construction works. All calculations used only linearity and the stated coalgebra/comodule identities, never multiplication on $C$ or cocommutativity.
